projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edward T. Bartkiewicz was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Edward T. Bartkiewicz. Mr. Bartkiewicz served in the U.S. Army. He's a veteran of D-Day. He served in the European Theater. His highest rank was PFC. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was interviewed at Mr. Bartkiewicz' home in Parma, Ohio, February 6, 2003. Ed was 77 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: I was living on West 86 Street, which is the far west side, and it's south of Dennison. We were sort of on different nationality area. I was Polish, went to a Polish school. There were Irish. There were Italian. There were Germans. We were mixed everything, and we had no problems. So I grew up there until -- I even went to school until I was drafted. I was still living there, so and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So how old would you have been on December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Eighteen years old.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you out of school?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Seventeen, right? Yeah, seventeen. Then I turned 18 in February, which will be shortly my birthday.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were still a senior in high school then?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were out of school?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: I was one of these that wanted to work and make some money. I had three brothers in service already, and I was kind of lonesome, I guess, and I was in a -- going in 11th grade and turning 18, and I didn't know there was going to be any picking of draft number or anything, but I had brothers that volunteered into the service that were -- one was younger than me. One was older than me. We represented the Marines, the Navy. Another brother was in the Army, and I was in the Army, and I was told specifically by my brother in the Marines do not join the Marines. They're too tough, and so I took his advice, and I -- even though I liked the Navy, I wanted to keep my feet on ground. So that's the choice that I took, and I was drafted.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When would that be? When were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: It was in May of 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Six months after Pearl Harbor approximately?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Something like that, yeah, and -- '43, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it '43?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay, so you were working about a year or so the first year of the war?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: About six months mostly, and I worked for Lamson and Sessions, which was a fastener industry here, and they already folded up, so -- but anyway, I was drafted there, and I was -- I went to Camp Shelby, Mississippi, and there was 69th Division was training recruits there, and I completed my basic training, and after I completed it, we were ready to be shipped out. We -- all we knew is the next destination was going to be Fort Kilmer, okay, in New York. And when it came time for me to go, they pulled me out of the ranks and they says that I had some sort of defect in my ear that they wanted to check. So I was around for a couple of weeks and bored. I lost all the buddies that I knew, and they came around and asked for paratrooper volunteer. So I volunteered, but I was rejected. I was too light. I only weighed about 110 pounds.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Too light to be a paratrooper?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, how exactly would that make a difference?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Well, the weight that you have evidently -- that you're going to have about 60 pounds on you when you jump out of the plane. I would probably crush myself on the ground. And two weeks later they come around for volunteers for the rangers. I volunteered for that, and they accepted me. From then on, it was get ready to go, and in probably a couple more weeks, I was in New York, and I was shipping out to go overseas, and again, not knowing exactly where we're going, but we knew we would take some ranger training in England, and we went all the way north from New York, and in a large convoy, and you could see ships all around you, and ours was one of the biggest ones. I think we had about six thousand troops on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So about when did you go overseas?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: I think there might be a date there. Okay. Regardless, it was -- it was before Easter. Okay. It was before Easter, and we went to Liverpool. We disembarked from the ship in Liverpool. It was night. All night we traveled from the north to the south, southern part of England, and we were dispatched at a town. From there, there was a mountain, and there was -- and I always remember the name of the town was Broughton, England. Okay, and it was on the -- if you look at our map, it's on the west coast of England. There was a mountain. That's where we camped, and that's where we did our training, and the training was like the special services, okay?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: And there were only about 53 of us that were there training. We would train on the beach. We would train demolitions. We would train climbing hills and going down hills. We would train booby traps. We would train swimming with full field pack and to a wall, climbing a rope wall, going over, and how to detect land mines. Talk about personnel mines and so forth. And training with a telephone pole. Ten fellows lay on the ground, they push a telephone pole on your hands, and now you're going to start your exercising. Which for me it was young and vigorous, so I didn't mind it. But when I think about a fellow that was 20 years older than me, it was more a little bit unusual.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there older guys in your outfit then?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yes, yes. There were some fellows that were probably about 35 or 45. Maybe not 45, but maybe 40. And so anyway, we trained for two months. Everything was on the double, and that means you don't walk any time. The officers or the leaders of the men, if you're a squad leader or whatever, you don't eat before your men do. You eat after they eat. And one was reprimanded for that in front of us, and we thought that was a pretty good idea. So -- and this -- after we would train, we would have to wash our clothes whatever that was dirty. And you can't wash clothes in ocean water, salt water. And we found that out the first day. Day one, they __ know that, so they didn't give us the soap. After awhile they gave us the soap.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what happens when you wash it in ocean water?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: It won't soap up at all, and you can't remove the dirt, okay? And the ocean water is -- you can float on it just a little bit easier than you can on a regular lake water. We completed that, and then we got to know the British pretty well in town and so forth and had a little time to maybe go to Red Cross station or something, get some doughnuts and go to a movie, and we went from there to a marshalling area, which is a point of demarcation when you're going to be going across the channel. And there were thousands and thousands of different people in vehicles and they had planes and everything. So we got familiar with that for about a week, and then it was time to debark for the invasion, and I -- I believe that we left on the 5th, early in the morning on the 5th. We were supposed to attack the beaches that morning, and which the time there when you're out in the middle of the channel, technically it can take you maybe 20 minutes to get to the beach by boat, and you can name any kind of boat you want to as far as landing crafts and battleships and everything. They were there, and loud and clear. The water was rough. We seen smaller landing crafts. I was in one with about 53 or 60 men. We were battling the waves, and they held us on the big ships before we manned the landing craft for that day because they changed it from June 5th to June 6th. Even though it was still -- the water was choppy and everything, they had to make that decision, and that little angel was sitting on my shoulder because we could see boats going down and under next to us and being hit by a large artillery or groundfire, and we just seemed to got through it all the way, but we were probably about two feet water depth when we stopped and we were stopped by these German -- oh, steel -- what do you want to call it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Obstacles?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Obstacles. And as soon as you stop, he would drop the front down and just everybody had to holler, Get Out, Get Out as fast as possible, because he wants to turn around and he wants to get out of there and maybe pick up some more men and come back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What beach did you land on?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: At Omaha.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You did land on Omaha, okay.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yeah. And I didn't look back at all until we were well on the beach, okay? And then I looked back, and it looked like a junkyard really. You could see the big ships really hammering way out in the distance, but everything else it looked like it was disorganized, okay? But it really wasn't. We were supposed to go in with the Second Ranger Battalion, which was on our right, and they was supposed to go the furtherest right, and we were supposed to sort of follow them and go to the left of them, and somehow we got separated, and maybe, maybe it was a good thing, or I don't know, but we got in. Then once we got on land, we sort of froze right there for a while until somebody would kick. They wouldn't actually kick you in the butt, but they said let's go, don't sit here because we're going to be sitting ducks. So we got closer. We had to go through barbed wire, and I assisted a fellow that came up with bazooka -- not bazookas, but they were long tubes. They had --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: They had -- and you could connect them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Explosive device?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yeah, explosives, and I helped them push that thing through the barbed wire, and then we had to back off, and he had the ignition mechanism to ignite it, and he would blow a hole in that barbed wire, and there were like three rolls of barbed wires there close together, and it was just enough for our troops to get through. Otherwise, we would have to just go and lay on them, and the rest of the guys would run across us and so forth, whatever, whoever. And we got through that, and again, we got close enough where they could not shoot at us because we were too close to them and they were high, and I'm sure they knew we were there, but they didn't -- it didn't bother them. So this lasted for most of the day, and then come evening, there was a -- Normandy said there's going to be a password, okay, that we use. Every day they give you a new password. And this day they didn't give us a password. They says all you had was a cricket. You know what a cricket is?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yeah. I had a hard time finding one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You still have one or did you --

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Well, my daughter got one for me, and I use this for my speeches.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: And so he says, once we get up on the top of the hill and settle down for that day, you don't -- you may even be there just five minutes and you get shot or -- well, you don't know. We don't know. So when it gets dark, you don't holler for anybody's name. You don't answer anybody with your name. You just -- you use this {made clicking sound} and you do it once and they have to do it twice {made clicking sound} and that way you both will know that you're communicating with the right party, and we used that the first day. We didn't use it after that. But I thought it was -- whoever thought it up was a pretty good idea, but we stayed right where we were that whole night, whether it was an hour or two hours that you got some shut-eye, didn't make any difference, and you weren't moving. But if anything was moving around you, you better shoot it, he says, because it's not going to be American because they are told just freeze right there, and then came next morning everything started all over again from day one. So it -- it just kept on going that way. And so the next day we got together, the fellows that we could see or get in contact with, and we counted all the fellows that were in our platoon that we trained with, and we started with 53 people and all we could count was 28. So we were sort of a bad shape there, and everybody felt bad about it, but you could see that there were a lot of damage done, a lot of soldiers killed, German and American, and like I say, the beach looked like a junkyard, I mean, massive, and everything was floating around, because I found out later that they were sinking our own ships to make a break wall. Otherwise, they couldn't come into shore where the engineers prepared for the removal of equipment from ships, and nobody ever told us, well, they're going to be bringing tanks in and so forth. We just thought there was going to be millions of troops coming in. So anyway --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yours was the Fifth Ranger Battalion?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What Company or --

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Company F, yeah, and we had -- our highest command was a colonel. Okay. We had no jurisdiction under a general or anything. And we had a major. His name was High Tower, and what appropriate name for something like that. Real good soldier and so forth. And so from there we liberated our first town, which wasn't too far. Maybe a thousand yards or so, and found out later that some of these places you thought were cities and villages were cardboard, and they were just painted and they looked like houses and they looked like grass and flowers and stuff. It was simulated. So we took some towns, and we saw -- took a lot of prisoners, and we saw the French celebrating. I think, within a week, there was a couple that got married right away. They knew what it was all about. So our destination was to go across France south, southwest and a cutoff the part of France. We were heading for Cherbourg, okay? There is a Cherbourg Peninsula, and there's also a Cherbourg town. The town is on the edge of Cherbourg in France, but if we cut that off, we would capture thousands and thousands of Germans. In that particular area was a town called Brest, which was ammunition dumps. It was submarine base, and it was for ships dockage and so forth, and we wanted to capture that, which we did finally get it, and once we got it, the prisoners started coming in by, not the hundreds, but the thousands. We didn't have men enough to even police them, to guard them. You had maybe four machine guns guarding three thousand prisoners. And somebody arranged us to take a hundred prisoners with ten Americans, and take them back down to the beach and release them to someone there and they would put them on a ship and send them over to England. Probably a lot of them wanted to go back to Germany, but that's beside the point. I found out they weren't all Germans. They were all nationalities, and I was talking to one in Polish, and he tried to say I'm not a German. Everything was in Polish, and he tried to tell me that he needs some milk, that he's forced to do this, and so forth, and I agreed with him, but I says I can't do it and I can't help you right now. We're in a war, and because I found out through communication of letter writing that my mother did in Poland in 1939 and so forth, 1940 and so forth. So anyway, when we took that part of France, it was a good hunk of France, we were doing all this with the prisoners. We were supposed to feed them here. We didn't have the food. We just pushed them to the next area and so forth, and we were supposed to go from there and start moving inward toward Germany from there, and -- but they wanted to clean up that area that we captured, which were a battery of pillboxes, which some of the pillboxes could go as deep as five, six, or seven stories down in the ground. They had their own water supply. They had their own electrical supply, generator. They had their own air- conditioners. They did not depend on anything that could be buried there. Well, that's what some of them were, and when they start digging up some of the stuff, it was like a springwater coming out. The Germans were coming out of the hole in the ground. So we were just loaded with taking prisoners, and then they gave us two days notice that they're going to blow up those docks and submarine basis and ammunition base. So in two days it was like two days of -- after that, it was like two days of 4th of July. I mean, it didn't cease, didn't stop. Just kept. We were probably ten or twenty miles away from it, and spectacular, you know. We were glad that it was happening, because later on, I found out that it's not easy to blow up a pillbox. I don't care how much dynamite you put in it. So we started going from there, we went south and started cleaning one town after another and hill after another hill. Oh, boy, let's take that town. We can stay there overnight, and we did. We got the town, but we didn't stay there overnight.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were the French people pretty nice to you that you encountered?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yes. We right away -- as soon as we liberated a town, the French people got all the French that collaborated with the Germans and shaved their hair off real quick, and the women had to walk either shaved or put a babushka on. They weren't hardly any men at all, and sometimes the people in the city would even hang the people right on the square right then and there. There was -- you could always find some kind of a food, the Americans, as I would scrounge it for food, and they always warn us don't eat none of the food. It's poison. I never gave it a thought. I mean, I just ignored it, and we had canned chicken. We had eggs. We had everything, bacon. We had ham. We would find it in different places. If you're traveling a hundred miles through the country, you're going to find an ear or two by the bundle, and then you start learning some of the language about how to tell the Germans to get out, and the French called them Bosch, and we learned a word moshnel (ph) when we're marching Germans from one place to another or capturing them. I personally didn't -- all we did was we encountered the Germans, and after we encountered them and captured them, they were turned over to somebody else behind us, because we were always on the front line. We did not worry about heavy artillery because they were shooting over our heads. Those big boys were in the back, and our artillery was shooting over our head, because they were shooting at the rear echelon of the Germans, wherever they were going. We had assumed or we had concurred the air space of probably a month or so after D-Day, which made it very comfortable for our bombers to go and drop bombs and pick targets and so forth. There was still dogfights regardless, and sometimes we would enjoy it and sometimes we wouldn't. Because I saw our P-38s just get blown right out of the sky. I saw bombers getting blown right out of the sky at maybe 25 or 30 thousand feet, and they wouldn't break ranks or anything. Even if a bomber got knocked down, they just kept right on going. So if they had five minutes of bombing, it was like five years in the infantry. So anyway, what else can I go to now? Oh, yeah, the rangers. After about six months, I was working with other troops, other organizations in the front lines, and we were sort of, if they needed something to be done, they would call us and we would tell them that we're going to try to do it. Like this one time they -- they encountered some pillboxes, and they asked us to take care of them. So in the night we took five-gallon cans of gasoline and -- or like a half a dozen of us and we would go to this pillbox, sneak up to it. We didn't have any weapons or anything that could make any noise, and we would put the cans on the side and open the top vent and let it drip down the steps and under the door into the pillbox, and when you have about five or six cans like that, it'd start flooding that area, and they weren't that much waterproof to my knowledge, and then when we accomplished our mission, we just threw a hand grenade in there and everything was closed up. And what happened after that, I don't know, but that was like a mission that we did and -- or go somewhere else and maybe clean out a church tower or something like that, which I had a job to do one time with a fellow, and I thought for sure that that's going to be the end of it because they loved to put spies in lookouts in the church towers and direct artillery from there. So I assumed that there were somebody there, and fortunately, there wasn't. If there was, I didn't find them, okay? And then we even took towns later on that we were in the town for about four or five days and they were still communicating with the Germans on radio. We could hear them, but we couldn't find a radio. And finally, I think after about the fifth or sixth day, somebody must have found it, and I don't know where, and silenced it. So those are things that you take it for granted. You're in a town and you're safe. Well, you're not. Well, once they're ready to go, they call on their troops and they didn't have to fire two or three rounds to hit that town. The coordinates were all set ahead of time for them. All they had one round to drop and that was it. They could blow the whole square up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that a German communicating or was that --

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: A German communicating.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Hiding out?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: And we assumed, because it was German talk, and not saying that there weren't some collaborators French giving the Germans and buying his way through the war, you know, or whatever. I don't know. Anybody could have been, but it becomes pretty dangerous. And we were going on across rivers, up mountains, back across the same river again and back again, and then going over another mountain, and the Germans were experts at putting dynamite around a tree of about six to eight inches diameter and have just enough dynamite that it would blow that tree and it would fall right across the road without breaking it off, and they could do that with about ten or twelve trees, and that would stop all transportation through that road whether it was tanks or whether it was kitchen, whether it was troops or whatever it was. We were on tanks one time and we encountered that. All the troops got off the tanks and just start walking right through it and passed it, and the tanks had to go probably to another city or village or something to get through. And another time we were on top of a mountain and -- on top of tanks and the infantry would always ride the tanks if they were available, and they didn't ask. They just jumped on them. And we were on the mountain and the first tank leading -- the road was just wide enough for the tank. And the first tank, the road gave away on it and it went bouncing down like a rubber ball down the side of the mountain, and probably about two hundred yards, and all I found out later on that the guys in the tank got killed, but some of our men -- you could see them jumping off the tank just about the time it was ready to roll, and our tank was the next tank. It stopped right there, and I says that little angel is over there sitting on my shoulder again, huh? I had that happen a lot of times. And we encountered a lot of mine fields, which I totally ignored. We ran right through the mine fields. We didn't even -- didn't even think about it. Maybe one out of a hundred would maybe step on a mine, but we encountered a pillbox. We were on a patrol, 12 of us. We encountered a pillbox, and at this particular time, I took a submachine gun, and I had two medic bags that carried -- each carried eight clips of ammunition. So I must have had about three or four hundred rounds of ammunition on me, and I figured, if somebody's going to shoot at me, they're going to go with me. So we encountered this pillbox, and one of the fellows stepped on a mine, and it like blew his heel off or his toes off or something, and then the other fellows went to help him, and they stepped on a mine, and then we improvised stretchers with our shirt, our jackets, and that, and we tried to get in. The medic was trying to help lift up one guy and he steps on a mine, gets hit right in the face. Here we got six wounded, and six fellows. In the meantime, I was shooting the submachine gun at the pillbox to keep it closed up, okay? And it worked. So after awhile, the only way we got out of there was to backtrack our footprints. There was snow there and we backtracked. We couldn't take the wounded with us. We took one or two I think we took with us, and we had to go across a little creek and up another hill, and finally, somebody sent a weasel up there, because it was -- it's like a little tractor, no wheels, just all track, and you could put a half a dozen wounded people on there. So they came over there and helped get the rest of the fellows out of there because we were probably exhausted and maybe do the wrong thing and so forth. So to my knowledge, they did get them out, and that's -- you always assume that they did get them out, you know, try to assume the opposite.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: If a weasel hit that kind of a mine, it wouldn't do much damage?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Probably crack the track, yeah, but they were personnel mines primarily. They were not for vehicles or not for anything else. Mines that were put in a road for tanks they would blow the track off the tank or crack it, break it so that disabled the tank. It wouldn't -- the tank could still fire a weapon, you know, guns and that, but if a tank was hit with one of our antitank guns, they could do a lot of damage to it, generally kill the guys inside. So it -- from there we went on and up and down mountains and taking towns and so forth. Sometimes it was not -- not too dangerous, and we somewhat enjoyed it, you know. Say, hey, let's take the next town. Hell with it. We ain't going to stay here. So we were doing that, and we were coming close to the German border, and from there you start encountering a lot of pillboxes and so forth. We got to the Siegfried Line. We dug in. Siegfried Line is like -- oh, I don't know, about 190 miles long, and it's depth could be the depth of two football fields long, and they were staggered. Our tanks couldn't get across because of the tiger teeth. Once they got on top of them, they were vulnerable, and don't forget the Germans knew exactly how to hit them with one shot only. They didn't have to practice. So they -- somehow they had to get -- I think they got engineers in there to remove some of the obstacles there to allow tanks to get through, and once they got through, it eased things. And at one time, we, the American -- when I say we, I mean the allies. We had captured 52 pillboxes behind the Siegfried Line, and we were there for over two months. They warned us that they're going to blow these pillboxes up, going to put 500 pounds of TNT in each one, and they're going to blow them up. Well, there was another short 4th of July. All these things were blown up. You could hear them 50 miles away, and after we blew them up, the next day the Germans were right back in them again. They didn't blow the tops off of them. All they did was crack them. That's how well constructed they were. I saw some of them in -- later on in operation where they were building these, and you would have a hard time sticking your hand straight down between the iron girders and that that they put in there. It had to be very fine cement that they keep pouring in there because they were so well inter wound, and I would always try to find it. If I found a German weapon or a French weapon or something, I would look it over. I would try to see how it worked or whatever. And I had never knew if I would be maybe captured with one of those weapons or a German weapon to know that I could use it to help me. And by this time, I had a P38 weapon on my side, and I had a Luger, and I gave it to one of the guys in the kitchen, and we were on Siegfried Line. We were being replaced after sitting there for a while. Things were just getting too quiet. And we could see the Germans and I would fire at the Germans. They were from probably a thousand yards away. I could see them running from one pillbox, and whenever I seen that, I would start firing at them, and I knew that they were aware of it because they would hit the ground. And then we were relieved by -- I was trying to figure out whether it's the 99 or 106 Infantry, or 108, guys that just came from the states, you know. You could see all -- everything was nice and green and so forth, and they were prodding through, walking through mud that was about eight to twelve inches deep and out there on the front lines, and I could just think to myself, boy, you're going to learn how to be a soldier in one day you go up there. We had bunkers eight foot by eight foot by eight foot, and we had everything on top of it. Even if you put a house on top, you would put it. We had trenches to every foxhole from there. We had hand grenades and rifle grenades by every foxhole, and when they came, they just I thought this was a war. I didn't think this was a party. So they took over and we moved back to the rear echelon and we assumed that we were getting a break. So we moved back and we went north from there. The Battle of the Bulge has just been starting to get organized by the Germans and we were in a secondary line of defense where we set up crossroads, machine guns on the crossroads and everything and infantry in between, and they says, if you want to dig us a foxhole, all right. If you don't, just do whatever you want to do. I think I dug one foxhole for the whole war, and I just cleaned a spot off, put some leaves on there, put some branches on there, put tarp on there, and just stayed there for that time. And so it was just starting to get dark and all of a sudden we heard some firing -- no, before that, I seen some of the American vehicles going up, jeeps, trucks, kitchen trucks pulling a stove and so forth, and it looked like some officers in jeeps even going up right through us. I said, where the hell they going? It's the front lines up there. And like nobody paid any attention to whatever you said or what you thought, and when it got dark, somebody started shooting. Well, when they start shooting, they were just across the road from us, okay? So we were as though we were waiting for them. We were all set up. The machine guns were set up. There was all kinds of ammunition flying in all different directions, and some of them -- our machine gun just could cut a person's body right in half if he was in front of that machine gun within 20 feet, okay? And that's what happened. This guy was ready. He was going to throw the hand grenade at the machine gun, and that was the end of it. It stopped right there, never let go of the hand grenade. So you know, it makes you feel good that we have got very brave people in our service all over. I don't care whether it's any service. And so we took a beating, not knowing that -- we knew that we encountered the Germans, but we didn't know. I think we were probably about five miles behind the front line at the time, and I have got maps and pictures and everything that shows all about it. So I captured a couple of Germans right in front of me. I had a German machine gun two feet in front of my nose when I opened my eyes, and I didn't know whether I should move or whether I should just freeze there, but I didn't see any Germans around it. I didn't see any ammunition around it. So it seemed like the guy with the machine gun came and set it up and was waiting for his ammunition bearer to come, and he probably never made it. So this guy retreated, and maybe I shot maybe over his head, I don't know, or by his ear, I don't know, that night. And the next morning I went, moved about ten feet to the -- not a gully but a lower spot in the road, on the side of the road. There were two Germans in there. One was laying face down, and the other one was looking up. He had his hand up with his gun in his hand, a Luger, but it wasn't moving. So I thought, well, maybe he's dead. So anyway, I just walked over there, took the gun out of his hand, and he says, "Comrade, Comrade." I was shocked, and then when I told him to get up, I walked him over, gave him to some other fellows. The other one turned over and he says, "Comrade, Comrade." So what the hell's going on here, you know? [END OF CD ONE; BEGIN CD TWO]

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yeah, so that we wouldn't, because a lot of times, when you take a beating, you just go around and start shooting all the body to make sure they're dead, okay? The Germans taught us that. So even when I first hit the beach, I saw one of our paratroopers hanging in a tree, 82d Airborne, and nobody took him down. The Germans used him as target practice and all that stuff, and it just boiled my blood, okay? I have never forgot it, and I never will. But anyway, we took him -- it was a kid maybe 15 or 16 years old. The other guy was probably 30 years old, and they took him back to interrogate them and so forth to find out what happened. Well, it wasn't long after that we pull out of there, because the Germans were bringing big tanks and heavy weapons and more infantry, and they were -- they knew they made a move there, so they're going to keep pushing it. So we went out of there and supposed to go into a village in the back of us, and Greneville was the town named there, and the Germans came up the road with their big tanks and everything. I didn't see any -- after awhile, I was looking for guys that were around there, and I know there were about 12 of us there, and this German tank went up there. It blasted our tank destroyer, blasted our trucks, blasted -- anything that looked like a vehicle, they just blew it out of sight, and not one but maybe three German tanks, but they didn't go away from the houses to check the foxholes around, and we just stayed down there. Hey, they don't know that we're here, just don't do nothing. That's when they around Melmody(ph) too, they took a whole bunch of prisoners. They took their shoes off. They had there -- and they took their jackets off. They had their hands like this. They were marching them, marching them right over an old knoll and just around the corner. And after that, all I heard was German machine guns buzzing. They just slaughtered them, all of them. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were near that when that happened?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yeah. And the Germans withdrew then. They -- they always don't stay necessarily in the places where they capture something, because they know that we're going to retaliate like with artillery or tanks or everything else. And in the evening, a truck came up there, one of American trucks, because it was sort of quiet and they probably wanted to find out what happened to all these other vehicles and stuff that they had to desert or left or were disabled, and we says where is everybody? What are you doing here? What are you doing here? I'm not playing cards, you know. And so we got on the truck and they took us, I don't know, maybe five miles back, dropped us off the truck and we joined some other Americans. I don't know who they were. It was dark. The town that we were going through there was just hit by German shells and everything. We saw Red Cross ambulances burning. We saw jeeps burning, houses burning and every -- guys in them, and I said why don't we go help them? They said don't break ranks, don't break. Because you're going to get lost and disabled and nobody's going to know where you are, whether you're a German or American. Somebody will take care of them, don't worry. So we just kept walking, walking. Must have walked for four or five hours. Finally, we got to a place where we could reassemble ourselves and so forth, and they tied us up with some other outfit. I don't know, part of the Third Army, I guess it was, and we got a break where we can take a -- breath a little bit, but that's when we realized that, hey, we're going the wrong way. What the hell's happening? So it's just --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you attached to the Second Division at this time?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: During the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: The rangers were -- let's see. What did their -- I can't -- they disbanded the rangers like six months after I was with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay, so that's when you were --

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Okay, and then they put me with the Second Division, and that's -- I was with the Second Division all that time, and so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Under Battle of the Bulge, on this, it says something about enemy, disguise, enemy, right there.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Oh, okay. We were -- we were put -- we went to a place on the hill and it was cold then. It was maybe ten degrees above zero snowing. We had about three foot of snow. Let's say two foot, but it seemed like three foot, and we were on this hill and the Germans were trying to take a dam there that they had set up, because if they could concur that dam and blow it up, it would wipe out a whole village down -- somewhere down and do a lot of damage to the Americans as far as they're concerned, because it probably had where the Americans were sitting in there and doing different things. So we were up there and the Germans were firing shots at us, and all of a sudden, this is where we got quite familiar with the Screaming Mimis. They were probably about eight inches in diameter, probably about three foot long or more, and when they fired on them, they went whoo, whoo, whoo, whoo, whoo, whoo. You could hear them, and once they got over your head, you were happy, you know. You know, oh, boy, keep going. I don't care, but they're going to hit something somewhere. And one of their large artillery guns hit in the foxhole right next to me where a fellow, my buddy, just dove into that foxhole when they heard the Screaming Mimi go across, and the shell hit right in that hole, and it didn't explode, and I was right next to him. I was probably about ten foot away from him. So it wasn't long after that we were trying to see what damage was done, and here they pulled a guy out of the hole out of his foxhole because he dove in like headfirst, and which I did too, and he had -- he had a cut on his nose. That's all he had, but he was in shock, okay, or maybe I was too. I don't know. But they took him to the back right away. After awhile, they dug that shell out, and it was about three foot high and it was about six inches or more in diameter, never exploded. It -- and they had a lot of those, because they had all these different people doing stuff, making them in different plants and so forth throughout Europe, you know, and the Germans were confiscating them. Maybe that shell was made four years ago. I don't know. But anyway, we were glad that it didn't. And from there, we -- we moved to another town, and we were on the outskirts of that town and we heard that the Germans were making another move, and they put us on a truck. They had a lot of tank mines there, land mines for tanks. They says don't even worry about burying her, just scatter them, scatter them. (Interview interrupted by phone ringing.)

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Okay, so when we went to this other town and I think the town was Krinkled (ph), and we were guarding it on the outside. I don't know how many infantry we had there, and we didn't have any tanks or anything, and a German -- we knew -- somebody knew that they were coming. So they had trucks with all these mines on, just followed the truck and just keep staggering them down the road, you know. Somebody's going to have to pick them up, you know, as far as we ran out of them, so which wasn't maybe, I don't know, a thousand yards or something like that. And sure enough, they come with a scout car, a half track and Germans sitting -- two Germans sitting on top of it with their machine guns and so forth like everybody watching me, we're going to scare the bees away. So they were coming and we had one rifle grenade with us and we were in the foxholes. We had ammunition. We had hand grenades. We had a 50-caliber machine gun by us, and they were coming up. This -- this half track came up and it was -- it was down lower than we were, and there was a part of the ground where -- a rise, and they were behind it, and when they came from behind it, that we were close vision of them, we had no alternative but decided that we're going to take a shot at it, and I helped with loading the grenade and that, and the fellow -- I didn't shoot it, but the other fellow shot it, and the grenade hit the ground first, bounced off the ground, and then hit the half track and really shook it up, okay? And the guys that were on it I assumed probably got killed. One fellow got from underneath it. There's a trapdoor underneath, and he starts running back with the -- to the Germans, and that's when we put the .50 caliber and we start chasing them with the .50 caliber not realizing that we're drawing tank fire very shortly, and -- but we chased him. We chased him. We didn't get him. We didn't hit him, but I'm not a .50 caliber guy. So anyway, it was an experience that one doesn't normally want to encounter, but it's nice to talk about it. So from then on, when we finished that, we got the hell out of there, and the Germans were reorganized because they could have assumed that there was a hell of a lot of Americans there and not knowing where they were when we would knock out the first vehicle that these guys are like scouts. And so anyway, I'm talking about it right here. I got it. I saw only one person run from the vehicle. So my buddy ran him down with a .50 caliber machine gun. To this day some of the Fifth Ranger training was loading and landing on the beach with a small -- no, that's something else. But anyway, we knew we were deep into Germany, and the Germans were looking for time, and I didn't know it then, but I know it now that all they wanted to do was make a penetration into the American army so they could have time to withdraw all of their guns, all their vehicles, all of their army and everything else, and we were capturing them on the way. Sometimes when we were on tanks going through -- I was in Ardennes force tool, and we were on tanks, and I was on a second tank again. I don't know why, but the first tank encountered two Germans and they had rocket guns, and they were in foxholes and they both shot, and I don't know whether they did it purposely or just bad shots, but they didn't hit the tank, and we knew what it was, and they got out of their foxholes naturally right away. All of the infantry jumped off the tanks and everything, and I started chasing. I must have chased this guy the distance of a football field before I caught him, okay? And I took care of him. So the other guy, I don't know. He went in the other direction, and it was just they can delay that whole convoy of tanks a half an hour or an hour or maybe longer because somebody didn't expect it, and what are we going to do now, you know? Instead of having everything planned and doing it, when you get encountered by the enemy like that, you have to change your decisions right away. So what I -- I see some of the paperwork I have here, and well, right after -- I don't want to spoil that course that I'm going through and so forth, but we start going into Sudetenland, and I knew Sudetenland was Czechoslovakia, all right? So I'm trying to listen to people talk and nothing but German, okay? And I would try to talk to them and they -- they didn't understand me. I was talking Polish or Czech, and I said this is supposed to be Czechoslovakia. Well, it's not, because they ran all the Czechs out of there and moved all the Germans in and became a German town, Sudetenland, all right? So anyway, we took that and we started going, and the things started getting a lot easier where we couldn't keep up the pace that the Germans were retreating, and we would stop in a town and we didn't -- we didn't see anything in front of us, so why should we go running after nothing? We would go in a town and we would find food, and this one town had a distillery. So one of the officers got in big trucks, and we loaded three trucks up with all of this liquor and everything and every soldier had liquor bottles in his pockets and in his shirt and every place else, and I think everybody slept for two days. So that's one of the good times that we generally have. Went onto, after Sudetenland, and we went into Czechoslovakia, a little bit of Austria. Some delays there battling, but was trying to establish, reestablish our position that was prematurely designed that before the breakthrough and we were getting close to it, and then we got into Czechoslovakia, and it's just -- the civilians were probably shooting at more Germans than the Americans were, but it was just -- we didn't have tanks and we went with the infantry. We went into Pilsen. We liberated it, and when we're on the street, I could look up at the fifth floor of an apartment and I can see a Czech shooting at a German running way down there somewhere, you know. I don't even know if he could hit him or what, but they did their best at what they could do to help us, you know, and the next day it was all party time, all dressed up in nationality clothing. Then when they found out that I could communicate with them, I got the main room right on the corner of the hotel, and on the other corner of the street that room was all cleaned out was an old bar and everything, and they just lined all the walls with kegs of beer because the Pilsen's brewery wasn't far from there, and beer was free for everybody. All you had to do was bring the bucket, whatever. And -- but it was really a lot of good time was there, and probably while I was there, I think our president died, President Roosevelt, and they sympathized with us. I went to dances with women there and they had lots of bands, lots of places to dance and everything. Food -- they would bring you food if you wanted it. I went swimming with some of the fellows. I said I ain't got a swimming suit. You don't need a swimming suit. So it was just waiting and waiting, and then they start catching the fellows and counting the points that they had for their service time and so forth, and I was single. I had a lot of points, and few of the fellows that were married and had children and so forth, they would get a point or two ahead of me. I said let them go. I says they got something to go back to really, you know, waiting this long. They were lucky, and so they went and they flew back home from Czechoslovakia. I don't know what way, how, and I went by boxcar, 40 in one they call it. Forty troops in one car, your baggage and everything, and just -- we'll just keep going until you get to your destination. So we went and we went to Le Havre eventually, and from there, we spent about a week or so there. Encountered a whirlwind which darn near tore all the tents up in the air. I think they may have lost a lot of paperwork from our source, and we finally got on a ship. The ship was a big one. I think it was about six thousand troops going back home. Took us 14 days to get there. Took us seven days to get back. The ship was the Monticello, and the Monticello word is on a nickel, and the nickel to me became very popular with the Monticello on it. I never forgot it. And got back to New York, and the Queen Mary was docked next to us before us. There were bands playing and everybody's hollering and everything. We pull in and like they turn all the lights down on us, you know, and we got off and I kissed the ground and I was glad. Well, I don't want to go on a ship again for a long, long time. And we had went to a place where they gave us a nice big steak and a nice big meal and everything, and they says that you'll be going to your -- another destination, which we knew I was going to Camp Swift, Texas, and yeah, what are we going to do there? Well, you're going to train to land in Tokyo. Thanks. I really needed that, you know. So anyway, that's what we found out, and we -- I got down there, and who was doing all the kitchen work and all the sweeping and all the grass cutting? German prisoners of war. That -- I didn't go with that too good. So we decided -- we were out on the second floor of this place where the Americans were staying. I said we're going to teach them a lesson, see if they can catch on something. We took all of our beds and everything. We just out the window, threw everything out, you know. Nobody ever said a darn word about it. The next morning that was all straightened up and -- but they had told -- no guards. They had all the freedom they wanted. They don't want to go anywhere. They're getting fed. They're getting sleep. They're getting not harassed or anything. So I was there for a while. And then I got a 30-day leave from there to go home. It was the first break I really got since I was in service, 30 days, and I came home. I says Higel(ph), I'm going to meet you in front of the terminal tower in Cleveland, because he was from Pennsylvania, but he was in Cleveland that particular day. And he says okay. So we planned on meeting there the next day and the war was over. I went down there -- or I wasn't looking for him. We just got in line and ran the battery down practically and enjoyed it and really glad that the war was over in Japan there. So from then on, I come home. I started a machine shop training in high school. I went back to a place that did that kind of work and I got a job. They moved from my backyard practically to a place on 150th, and it's still standing there, and I became a good machinist, and I became lead man and foreman and tool engineer there. So it was profitable for me. I enjoyed it and had -- my wife had five girls and a boy, and I have got 13 grandchildren and I did -- we do a lot of service for churches, societies, and so forth. I was with the Catholic War Veterans for, oh, about 15 years. We used to have the color guard going to the cemeteries and all that stuff, and something drastic happened and that sort of got washed away, and so it was quite silent for a while. No -- there weren't many people shaking your hand or waking you up that how did you do in the war? How did you do this? It was a silence of about 20 years, and after that, they start digging out, figuring out who are these veterans that did all this fighting and so forth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies over there when you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yeah, but he just passed away. His name was -- his name is Perry. I got it somewhere here. I got to find it now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would you and he do for distraction or to relieve the tension between combat?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Well, I didn't smoke, and after I was in one of the first battles, they would give us a little package of cigarettes and a little package of gum and a chocolate bar candy in your rations. Well, I could get two candy bars for three cigarettes. So I never threw the cigarettes away. I was carrying them until the crucial part where nobody had them and they were worth more and I would trade them off. So a lot of times I understand we were supposed to get like a hot meal a day. Well, how can you get a hot meal a day on the front line? I didn't come there to get shot at. I come there to feed you, and if they're going to shoot at me, I'm not going there. So if we didn't have a hot meal and we knew the kitchen crew was walkable distance, we would slaughter a cow or chickens, or whatever, anything. You had the most finest butchers from the south that you can ever want, and they would take a cow and walk them in a barn and an hour later they would come out with all the meat, and they just loved what they were doing. So when the kitchen needed meat, somehow somebody found a way of getting food to them regardless of what it was. Never -- I never worried about poison or nothing like that, never did. I was just lucky. And you didn't hear much about anything like that so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They were afraid that the Germans had left behind poison food. Is that --

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Setting us up, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: I was trying to think of that. Rangers deactivated six months after, and then they were reactivated later on just before the end of the war, and -- but I never got any call or anything like that, and like I -- I -- some things that I didn't talk about and I have in here I notice, my brother that was in the Army he was fighting in Italy, and Northern Italy and Austria, and I was fighting north of that maybe three, four, five hundred miles, and my brother younger than him was in the Marines and he was a Marine raider and special, and he got killed on Iwo Jima just two days before they concurred it, and then I had another brother that was in the Navy and he was out of Philadelphia and he was on ships going here and there, and I had four brothers -- brothers-in-law. I wasn't married yet, but my wife's brothers, four of them were in services, Air Corps, two were in the Navy, and one was in the Army, so a lot of representation.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I see a note here hedgerows suicide?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Okay. A lot of people did not know what hedgerows were, and for many, many years, and I tried to explain even to kids -- they are more interested in it than older people. The hedgerows started when people had it, in my opinion, and I saw it on even Discovery Channel there -- that when people set up a property and build a house and they would line it with rocks and so forth and plant little shrubs and so forth, that's their property, and if they had an opening there, there was another one behind where the cattle were fed and grazing and so forth. Well, every time they would cultivate this property, they would find rocks and they would keep stacking them up high. Well, after awhile, the roads became embedded and lower, and when it rained, it was all muddy. So they would walk on the hedgerow, which was dry, and as it grew up higher, they kept using it, and then after awhile, the roads were probably reconditioned where they didn't have the water standing on them, the cattle, or a lot of oxen and a lot of stuff like that. They weren't driving cars when we were going through there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: And I tell them, I says, those hedgerows can vary from one-foot high to four-foot high, five-foot high, very convenient for a soldier to lean up against it, open the area up for vision and start shooting, okay? And I was -- I was fortunate that one time we -- right at the beginning of the war, we were going through some hedgerows and I heard a German machine gun open fire, and we were all in line against this hedgerow and he was coming right down it, and I just jumped right over this hedgerow, and I never found out if I was the only one that survived or how many got wounded or anything like that. I never seen those people again, because I don't know if you know it, but -- and they don't mention it too often how fast a German machine gun fires. It's like three times as fast as the American. When a German machine gun fires, it's one solid streak, and every fourth shot is a tracer. When our machine guns fire, you could count the tracer bullets more or less. Ours goes too-too-too-too {making sound}, and theirs goes burr, burr {making sound}. So I thought I would just throw that in there. But I was -- I was very proud of the Second Division. I was proud of the rangers. I -- I thought I had real good training before I went to England, and when I was there and I had working with explosives and booby traps and all that stuff, I found out how little I knew about training to -- of survival and so forth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned losing what, about half the platoon on D-Day?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies that day?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: I never heard if we got any of those guys back. So I figured we lost about 28 guys, okay? And even though we thought we were on the extreme looking at the beach from the water at the extreme right, but there were a lot of other ships down there, but we were heading for that cliff, okay? And if you got close enough to that cliff, you were safe, okay? They could not shoot at it. You had -- but they had a large gun up there. And the Second Ranger Battalion went up there and they found out that it was abandoned already, and I came back there taking troops back down to the beach and so forth. This was like maybe a month or two months later, and I looked at that cliff that they wanted us to scale and so forth, and some of them did scale it, but there was a thousand-pound bomb hanging there. You know, they were just waiting for the right time to get those troops down there, and they would just drop that bomb right -- they just un-tach it, you know. And that's the way they do it. The Germans were clever, very clever. I -- I never called them stupid, dummies, or anything, because they -- they were very clever. When they backed into a town or left a town and they would go into a village, you could take the cover off the sewer in the middle of the village and it would have a picture of what you just left on the wall and all the coordinates for a mortar to sit and hit a spot with one shot. It was just very smart, and I have had -- I have captured officers and they come up to me, how stupid you Americans are. Look at you. You're using our weapons, a sidearm, you know, and you know, I called it a souvenir, but he says no, you could use your own. You don't have to use ours. And -- and right there, it boiled your blood, and he wouldn't back off. Everything -- they had real good helmets.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you do a lot of souvenir collecting?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Do what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you do much souvenir collecting?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: No, because right at the beginning, one of my buddies -- he went in a house and he found a whole box of silver, sterling silver, okay? And he put it in his backpack and he was going to take it along with him, maybe get a chance to put it in the rear echelon somewhere. Well, he didn't get very far. The next battle we entered he got killed right away, and I thought I don't even ever want anything like that, you know, on my back or anything. I ain't saying that it drew something, but it's just a coincidence, but I have had fellows, they're standing right in front of me with their back toward me and they would get the bullet and get killed, and there's nothing that I could do. And another one would get shot in the shoulder or something like that and he would fall down, and I would say -- I would go over and I would try to help him, and all of a sudden they're shooting at us. Whoever it was they could see us very well. So he was sort of, I don't know, unconscious or something, the fellow that got shot, and I wasn't maybe four foot away from him. So I tried to hook the site of my rifle in his shoelaces or clothes and pull him over where I was because I was safe. They could shoot, but they couldn't shoot me as long as I didn't stick my head out. So they saw -- they must have seen that I was trying to do -- help him or something and they just riddled him with bullets right away, and I just -- I had a radio with me, not that I -- it was just by chance I had a radio, and I told him, I said, get some damn tanks up here and blow that tower off of that church. And just about that time, they had smaller mortars than we did, and they could like shoot right across the street there, and they were trying to get me by shooting just over that mound that I was behind, and I -- I see that they was zeroing in. So I just took the radio and I smashed it all up and I took off in lower ground and got out of there safely. So I was very fortunate. I never was wounded. I had a shrapnel metal stuck right in my belts over here from some shells that burst up in the air. You know, it hits you, and I'm looking, what the hell, there's a shrap metal there, you know. I should have kept it, but I didn't. And there's so many times people saved my lives, many times. I was in a -- I was by the Siegfried Line. I was drinking some pop out of a can, and I -- my eyes were level with the ground and I put the can up a little bit higher. Well, somebody shot a hole right through that can, and I thought what if I was drinking that can right then, you know? And another time where we took a village and it was -- it looked like an airport, but it was so flat and they had artillery, German artillery piece and an antiaircraft gun and they leveled it and they used it like a rifle and they could time the shells to burst wherever they wanted to, and we had just taken that and I took -- I went upstairs. I says, I'm going -- I think I'm going to take this room for tonight, you know, and I hung my belt on my backpack on there and went down. Let's see if we could find some food, and all of a sudden kaboom. The top of the house was blown off. Just seconds, you know, I was there and gone, and that teach you don't fight for a room in any house anywhere. So it -- it's really, you know, amazing that when you can go through all of that. Leipzig -- I was in Leipzig. I was in -- by the Melmody(ph). I was in by crossing the Rhine River. I saw the plane that came in. It was a jet, German jet and dropped a bomb on the bridge by the Rhine River and disabled the bridge because trucks could drive across it prior to that. Well, we were on top of a ridge. I don't know, maybe 2,000 feet, you know, higher. It was way down. And later on, we had to cross that river. So they called in the Navy, and they brought like lifeboats you could put 12 or 13 fellows in, powerful motor in the back. The Rhine River is a very, very fast river, and they loaded us up in there, and when they started going away from shore, the boat was going backwards. He couldn't fight the current of the river. Well, he couldn't go across because he don't know where he's going to end up over there. He might end up in camp with the Germans over there, and so they had to wait and they got either cables or something and were holding these boats from going away and motor running and we got across that way. Then they built pontoon bridges, and when one vehicle went across, it was all right. But if you got three or four vehicles and the middle sank down, the river says bye-bye. We'll see you never, and it just ripped that pontoon bridge all to hell, and I got books and pictures and everything of it. So it's -- and people now, you know, they want to hear about this and so forth. And it's -- it took me awhile before I could start getting things together so that I could make a good speech. I gave it to AARP and they loved it, and I gave it to veterans organizations and the schools and Medina and Bryan, and I'm not afraid to talk about it, but you just got to -- you have to sort of plan it to the type of people that you're speaking to. This one time we stayed in this town and the artillery moved up and they had these long guns. They must be -- the barrel must be 50 feet long, and they charge it up with powder and everything, barrel straight up. When it -- when they blew that first shot, everything went down about a foot, you know, all these big steel plaques and everything, and then once they was set in Nog(ph), they can set their coordinates and start firing, probably shoot about 20 miles or more, and I was just about set on my ass. I didn't expect it, and they come through a town. They had to knock a corner of a house off just to make the turn. That's how big they were, but you know, I was very shocked, and it may have hurt my ear a little bit or made it the condition that it is, because I didn't -- the guys probably should have said you better plug your ears up or something like that, because I was probably 30 feet away from it, and it was so loud, my god, I don't know what the hell happened, you know. Did I tell you about the Polish prisoner that was in the first -- one of the first ones that I got to talk to? They were conversing in Polish, three of them, and I heard everything that they were saying. So I says, how are you, and I'm American, but I speak Polish and I would like to know where you learned -- why you're speaking Polish because we're from Poland. We were forced here. I said what did you do with your ammunition? You have no ammunition. He said I buried it way back there, and if they say anything, I'll say I ran out of ammunition, and they didn't want to kill anybody and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: These are the guys that you captured at D-Day?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Well, no, it was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A little later than that?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Maybe a week -- yeah, about a week after that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Somewhere in Normandy?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Bartkiewicz
sp.p: Yeah, so it -- it made me feel warm, and even though I was too hard crusted as a soldier to sympathize with them, I says somebody will take care of you, just keep telling them that, you know. [END OF CD TWO]
